title: Bigheads
blurb: An attempt to smuggle an artwork into a game. Built at Manchester Innovation Lab to test how far the fidelity of the web can be pushed, it takes Pac-Man as its shape and a photograph of your face as its hero. You steer by tilting the phone. The camera is the way in. The participatory tactics of our installations, carried into a retro arcade game, and a way to learn what makes games work.

title: TILO v2
blurb: The second generation of TILO, our hybrid display system for arts and cultural venues, built for Phoenix in Nottingham. Most venue screens broadcast at people. TILO holds a dialogue with them instead, personal and aware of its context. Version two rebuilt the platform on a decade of lessons from the original, and launched by putting a 2014 artwork back on it. When I Grow Up was restaged on a screen good enough to do it justice.

title: Fantasia Express
commissioner: Innovate UK - First of a Kind
blurb: Twelve months of research into location-based augmented reality inside a moving train carriage, funded by Innovate UK's First of a Kind programme with LNER. It ended in a two-week public trial on the East Coast Main Line, connecting passengers to the landscape passing outside and proving train travel could be a shared experience rather than a private scroll. Actually, that is a lie. The Fantasia Express is an alien spaceship sent to collect relics of our imagination, a cross between Predator and The Hitch-hiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
credits: With LNER, Corporation Pop and Immersive Storylab

title: BIGMOUTH
blurb: A cross between a confessional and Room 101, made for Metal's Liverpool Provocations. People told the BIGMOUTH what they felt was wrong with the world or their life, then looked through an eyepiece on the side of the installation and watched their words become the mouth of a small demon who carried the burden away. Speech shown not as audio but as the physical movements of a mouth, which meant the most private thoughts could be said in public and stay secret.
credits: Demon illustrations by Tomo. Spherical projection with Pufferfish Displays

title: Cakenocake
blurb: A weekend on Liverpool's high street with a signboard and no technology at all. Each question had two answers. GOD or NO GOD, cake or no cake, and which side of the street you walked was how you voted. The purest interface we've ever built is a pavement. People who would never touch a gallery installation found themselves taking a public position on the way to the shops, and arguing about it with strangers.

title: Emofie
blurb: Selfies crossed with emojis. A mobile app and a gallery installation in one, made with Phoenix in Leicester. Strangers perform an emotion for the camera, watch it become something daft and shareable, and walk on. It's just a piece of art. You look at it, play with it, share it and keep walking. For family, friends, colleagues, on a date or going solo. A small reminder that underneath the performance we are all basically the same.

title: When I Grow Up
blurb: Children picked a future self on an iPad, career, age and appearance, and watched a hand-drawn avatar of it mirror their movements across the cafe video wall. When they left, the avatar stayed behind for the next visitor to wear. Jump, and you swapped into someone else's abandoned future. Made for Phoenix's Sparks children's festival in 2014, and brought back nine years later to launch TILO v2.

title: TILO
commissioner: Digital R&D Fund for the Arts
blurb: A hybrid display system for arts and cultural venues, funded by the Digital R&D Fund for the Arts. An attempt to make the screens in an arts building talk back. TILO knew the time, the weather and the programme, and used them to talk with visitors rather than broadcast at them. Permanent installations followed at FACT in Liverpool, at Phoenix in Leicester and at Unilever's Port Sunlight, a collaboration between artists, arts organisations and industry.
credits: With Amaze and Pixel Inspiration. Research by the Creative Exchange, Lancaster University. Music: Luke Howard

title: The Humble Market
blurb: Lead artists on a collaboration between four Brazilian and UK artists. A trading floor for the things that can't be traded. It ran as a summer exhibition at FACT, as a performance event under a railway arch in Preston for the London 2012 Cultural Olympiad, and at the 2014 World Cup in Belo Horizonte, where the Brazilian Ministry of Culture selected it for the national arts programme. With ZU UK, a replica Rio taxi, a fake radio station and an Intimatron.

title: MeYouAndUs
commissioner: FACT · BBC Big Screens · Robots and Avatars
blurb: The series the practice is named after. A set of adaptable interactive artworks built to meet the public wherever a screen could be found. It ran on BBC Big Screens in Manchester, Leicester and Edinburgh, in a town square in Miguel Pereira, Brazil, at FACT in Liverpool, and in Robots and Avatars, a European touring exhibition. The same idea each time, strangers briefly connected through a screen that belongs to no one, reshaped for every new context.

title: Not the Beatles Tour
blurb: A walking tour of Liverpool that refuses to mention the obvious. The city's other stories, the ones that never made the museum circuit, triggered by location on people's own phones as they walk. No app store, no headset, no guide with an umbrella. The streets decide what you hear next. Self-initiated and at prototype stage.

title: Homewalk
blurb: A walk between where you are and where home is, made with Phoenix in Nottingham alongside people who have made that journey the hard way. A route traced on your own phone becomes a shared act of remembering. Every step of an ordinary street is walked in parallel with someone whose way home was measured in borders rather than bus stops.

title: Kindred Spirits
blurb: An evening takeover of Tate Liverpool built from Mondrian, with the Tate Collective and the Costumologists. Visitors chose one of four coloured tickets, each a feeling drawn from Mondrian's writings, made costumes, sat for photobooths, and were led on tours that ended at our installation on the fourth floor. Thirty-six screens, fed by thirty-six Raspberry Pis over half a kilometre of cable. Scanning your ticket summoned your portrait alongside everyone else who chose the same colour. Audio commissioned from Kepla.
credits: With Tate Collective and the Costumologists. Audio by Kepla

title: Sonic Market
blurb: A permanent public installation for Brighton Digital Festival that turns a working market into an instrument. Every hour the market's own sounds are collected, bent by live weather data, and returned quietly to the space that made them. On a stormy day the market plays differently than in sunshine. Most people never notice it's there. That's the point. The market simply sounds slightly more like itself.

title: Invisible Arts Network
blurb: A six-month residency for Rural Media, mapping the art already happening in a county that doesn't call it art. It launched with The Happening, a day conference that turned into a public party, celebrating 1960s psychedelia through 360 cinema, virtual reality and digital art, with a lot of help from Mash Cinema.

title: Handprint 2012
blurb: An online artwork, a series of live interventions and a mass-participation finale for the North West's Cultural Olympiad. The web component lived inside WE PLAY, the region's London 2012 legacy programme, and visualised the connections of everyone taking part. It ended over four September nights in Avenham Park, Preston, where four projectors and two scanning stations threw hundreds of freshly scanned hands onto a railway bridge. The happiest accident of the project was that the hands appeared to rise out of the water.
credits: Part of WE PLAY, the North West's London 2012 legacy programme

blurb: A permanent installation in the waiting room of a new-build NHS health centre on Townsend Lane, Liverpool. Seventy-two local people were filmed waiting at the bus stops outside on hot summer days, and they now wait on screen alongside the people waiting inside. Bus routes are the arteries of a neighbourhood, and waiting became companionable. Community engagement was led by tenantspin. The title is the number of the buses that pass the door.
credits: Community engagement led by tenantspin with ABCC

title: Wishing Well
blurb: A permanent interactive installation in the courtyard garden of a new-build health centre on Mere Lane, Liverpool. The sister commission to 26:14:17, made through the same programme of community workshops for the Decade of Health and Wellbeing. A digital wishing well for a place where people arrive carrying wishes they don't usually say out loud.

title: Lowry to Life
blurb: Two linked installations on opposite sides of the city, built from L.S. Lowry's 1954 painting of Piccadilly Gardens and commissioned to mark the University of Salford's move to MediaCityUK. Each installation reflected a different perspective on the painting, connected telematically across Salford. Lowry's crowds were brought to life by the descendants of the people he painted. Covered by the Guardian and the BBC.

title: Handprint
blurb: For four December evenings, passers-by left giant handprints on City Tower, the 107-metre block in Piccadilly Gardens. Briefly, Manchester's most distinctive canvas. The first Handprint, funded by Arts Council England, and the work everything under that name grew from. The same gesture returned four years later to close the North West's Cultural Olympiad.
